entries.72340ef209cac123d61b77a017cc15b5c6ff07b9: <div sID="gen19076" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="34" osisID="Ezek.34" sID="Ezek.34"/> <div eID="gen19076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19077" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19078" type="x-p"/> The iniquities and calamities of God's Israel had been largely and pathetically lamented before, in this book. Now in this chapter the shepherds of Israel, their rulers both in church and state, are called to an account, as having been very much accessory to the sin and ruin of Israel, by their neglecting to do the duty of their place. Here is, I. A high charge exhibited against them for their negligence, their unskillfulness, and unfaithfulness in the management of public affairs, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.1-Ezek.34.6">ver. 1-6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.8">ver. 8</reference>. II. Their discharge from their trust, for their insufficiency and treachery, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.7-Ezek.34.10">ver. 7-10</reference>. III. A gracious promise that God would take care of his flock, though they did not, and that it should not always suffer as it had done by their mal-administrations, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.11-Ezek.34.16">ver. 11-16</reference>. IV. Another charge exhibited against those of the flock that were fat and strong, for the injuries they did to those that were weak and feeble, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.17-Ezek.34.22">ver. 17-22</reference>. V. Another promise that God would in the fulness of time send the Messiah, to be the great and good Shepherd of the sheep, who should redress all grievances and set every thing to rights with the flock, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23-Ezek.34.31">ver. 23-31</reference>.
entries.7f380d83471e653eacb73def014063f8306e8ff4: <div eID="gen19078" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19077" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Shepherds Reproved. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19079" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> unto the shepherds; Woe <hi type="italic">be</hi> to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks? <hi type="super">3</hi> Ye eat the fat, and ye clothe you with the wool, ye kill them that are fed: <hi type="italic">but</hi> ye feed not the flock. <hi type="super">4</hi> The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them. <hi type="super">5</hi> And they were scattered, because <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no shepherd: and they became meat to all the beasts of the field, when they were scattered. <hi type="super">6</hi> My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and upon every high hill: yea, my flock was scattered upon all the face of the earth, and none did search or seek <hi type="italic">after them.</hi> <div eID="gen19079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19080" type="x-p"/> The prophecy of this chapter is not dated, nor any of those that follow it, till <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.1-Ezek.40.49">ch. xl.</reference> It is most probable that it was delivered after the completing of Jerusalem's destruction, when it would be very seasonable to enquire into the causes of it. <div eID="gen19080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19081" type="x-p"/> I. The prophet is ordered to <hi type="italic">prophesy against the shepherds of Israel</hi>—the princes and magistrates, the priests and Levites, the great Sanhedrim or council of state, or whoever they were that had the direction of public affairs in a higher or lower sphere, the kings especially, for there were two of them now captives in Babylon, who, as well as the people, must have their transgressions shown them, that they might repent, as Manasseh in his captivity. God has something to <hi type="italic">say to the shepherds,</hi> for they are but under-shepherds, accountable to him who is the great <hi type="italic">Shepherd of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Ps. lxxx. 1</reference>. And that which he says is, <hi type="italic">Woe to the shepherds of Israel!</hi> Though they are shepherds, and shepherds of Israel, yet he must not spare them, must not flatter them. Note, If men's dignity and power do not, as they ought, keep them from sin, they will not serve to exempt them from reproof, to excuse their repentance, or to secure them from the judgments of God if they do not repent. We had a <hi type="italic">woe to the pastors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.23.1">Jer. xxiii. 1</reference>. God will in a particular manner reckon with them if they be false to their trust. <div eID="gen19081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19082" type="x-p"/> II. He is here directed what to charge the shepherds with, in God's name, as the ground of God's controversy with them; for it is not a causeless quarrel. Two things they are charged with:—1. That all their care was to advance and enrich themselves and to make themselves great. Their business was to take care of those that were committed to their charge: <hi type="italic">Should not the shepherds feed the flocks?</hi> No doubt they should; they betray their trust if they do not. Not that they are to put the meat into their mouths, but to provide it for them and bring them to it. But <hi type="italic">these</hi> shepherds made this the least of their care; they <hi type="italic">fed themselves,</hi> contrived every thing to gratify and indulge their own appetite, and to make themselves rich and great, fat and easy. They made sure of the profits of their places; they did <hi type="italic">eat the fat,</hi> the <hi type="italic">cream</hi> (so some), for he <hi type="italic">that feeds a flock eats of the milk of it</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.7">1 Cor. ix. 7</reference>), and they made sure of the best of the milk. They made sure of the fleece, and <hi type="italic">clothed themselves with the wool,</hi> getting into their hands as much as they could of the estates of their subjects, yea, and <hi type="italic">killed those that were</hi> well <hi type="italic">fed,</hi> that what they had might be fed upon, as Naboth was put to death for his vineyard. Note, There is a woe to those who are in public trusts, but consult only their own private interest, and are more inquisitive about the benefice than about the office, what money is to be got than what good to be done. It is an old complaint, <hi type="italic">All seek their own,</hi> and too many <hi type="italic">more than their own.</hi> 2. That they took no care for the benefit and welfare of those that were committed to their charge: <hi type="italic">You feed not the flock.</hi> They neither knew how to do it, so ignorant were they, nor would they take any pains to do it, so lazy and slothful were they; nay, they never desired nor designed it, so treacherous and unfaithful were they. (1.) They did not do their duty to those of the flock that were distempered, did not strengthen them, nor heal them, nor bind them up, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.4">v. 4</reference>. When any of the flock were sick or hurt, worried or wounded, it was all one to them whether they lived or died; they never looked after them. The princes and judges took no care to right those that suffered wrong or to shelter injured innocency. They took no care of the poor to see them provided for; they might starve, for them. The priests took no care to instruct the ignorant, to rectify the mistakes of those that were in error, to warn the unruly, or to comfort the feeble-minded. The ministers of state took no care to check the growing distempers of the kingdom, which threatened the vitals of it. Things were amiss, and out of course, every where, and nothing was done to rectify them. (2.) They did not do their duty to those of the flock that were dispersed, that were driven away by the enemies that invaded the country, and were forced to seek for shelter where they could find a place, or that <hi type="italic">wandered</hi> of choice upon <hi type="italic">the mountains and hills</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.6">v. 6</reference>), where they were exposed to the beasts of prey and became <hi type="italic">meat to them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.5">v. 5</reference>. Every one is ready to seize a waif and stray. Some went abroad and begged, some went abroad and traded, and thus the country became thin of inhabitants, and was weakened and impoverished, and wanted hands both in the fields of corn and in the fields of battle, both in harvest and in war: <hi type="italic">My flock was scattered upon all the face of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.6">v. 6</reference>. And they were never enquired after, were never encouraged to return to their own country: <hi type="italic">None did search or seek after them.</hi> Nay, <hi type="italic">with force and cruelty they ruled them,</hi> which drove more away, and discouraged those that were driven away from all thoughts of returning. <hi type="italic">Their</hi> case is bad who have reason to expect better treatment among strangers than in their own country. It may be meant of those of the flock that went astray from God and their duty; and the priests, that should have taught the good knowledge of the Lord, used no means to convince and reclaim them, so that they became an easy prey to seducers. Thus were <hi type="italic">they scattered because there was no shepherd,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.5">v. 5</reference>. There were those that called themselves shepherds, but really they were not. Note, Those that do not do the work of shepherds are unworthy of the name. And if those that undertake to be shepherds are <hi type="italic">foolish shepherds</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.15">Zech. xi. 15</reference>), if they are proud and above their business, idle and do not love their business, or faithless and unconcerned about it, the case of the flock is as bad as if it were without a shepherd. Better no shepherd than such shepherds. Christ complains that his flock were <hi type="italic">as sheep having no shepherd,</hi> when yet the scribes and Pharisees <hi type="italic">sat in Moses' seat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.9.36">Matt. ix. 36</reference>. It is ill with the patient when his physician is his worst disease, ill with the flock when the shepherds drive them away and disperse them, <hi type="italic">by ruling them with force.</hi>
entries.7bcb166267a77106baa9e726ceeefd9a0c2cca8c: <div eID="gen19082" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Shepherds Reproved. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19083" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore, ye shepherds, hear the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> I live, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , surely because my flock became a prey, and my flock became meat to every beast of the field, because <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no shepherd, neither did my shepherds search for my flock, but the shepherds fed themselves, and fed not my flock; <hi type="super">9</hi> Therefore, O ye shepherds, hear the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; <hi type="super">10</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> against the shepherds; and I will require my flock at their hand, and cause them to cease from feeding the flock; neither shall the shepherds feed themselves any more; for I will deliver my flock from their mouth, that they may not be meat for them. <hi type="super">11</hi> For thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I, <hi type="italic">even</hi> I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out. <hi type="super">12</hi> As a shepherd seeketh out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep <hi type="italic">that are</hi> scattered; so will I seek out my sheep, and will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. <hi type="super">13</hi> And I will bring them out from the people, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them to their own land, and feed them upon the mountains of Israel by the rivers, and in all the inhabited places of the country. <hi type="super">14</hi> I will feed them in a good pasture, and upon the high mountains of Israel shall their fold be: there shall they lie in a good fold, and <hi type="italic">in</hi> a fat pasture shall they feed upon the mountains of Israel. <hi type="super">15</hi> I will feed my flock, and I will cause them to lie down, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">16</hi> I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up <hi type="italic">that which was</hi> broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but I will destroy the fat and the strong; I will feed them with judgment. <div eID="gen19083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19084" type="x-p"/> Upon reading the foregoing articles of impeachment drawn up, in God's name, against the shepherds of Israel, we cannot but look upon the shepherds with a just indignation, and upon the flock with a tender compassion. God, by the prophet, here expresses both in a high degree; and the shepherds are called upon (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.7">v. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.9">9</reference>) to <hi type="italic">hear the word of the Lord,</hi> to hear this word. Let them hear how little he regards them, who made much of themselves, and how much he regards the flock, which they made nothing of; both will be humbling to them. Those that will not <hi type="italic">hear the word of the Lord</hi> giving them their direction shall be made to hear the word of the Lord reading them their doom. Now see here, <div eID="gen19084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19085" type="x-p"/> I. How much displeased God is at the shepherds. Their crimes are repeated, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.8">v. 8</reference>. God's flock became a prey to the deceivers first that drew them to idolatry, and then to the destroyers that carried them into captivity; and these shepherds took no care to prevent either the one or the other, but were as if there had been <hi type="italic">no shepherds;</hi> and therefore God says (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.10">v. 10</reference>), and confirms it with an oath (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am against the shepherds.</hi> They had a commission from God to feed the flock, and made use of this name in what they did, expecting he would stand by them. "No," says God, "so far from that, <hi type="italic">I am against them.</hi>" Note, It is not our having the name and authority of shepherds that will engage God for us, if we do not the work enjoined us, and be not faithful to the trust reposed in us. God is <hi type="italic">against them,</hi> and they shall know it; for, 1. They shall be made to account for the manner in which they have discharged their trust: "<hi type="italic">I will require my flock at their hands,</hi> and charge it upon them that so many of them are missing." Note, Those will have a great deal to answer for in the judgment-day who take upon them the care of souls and yet take no care of them. Ministers must <hi type="italic">watch</hi> and work as those that <hi type="italic">must give account,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">Heb. xiii. 17</reference>. 2. They shall be deprived <hi type="italic">officio et beneficio—both of the work and of the wages. They shall cease from feeding the flock,</hi> that is, from pretending to feed it. Note, It is just with God to take out of men's hands that power which they have abused and that trust which they have betrayed. But, if this were all their punishment, they could bear it well enough; therefore it is added, "<hi type="italic">Neither shall the shepherds feed themselves any more,</hi> for <hi type="italic">I will deliver my flock from their mouth,</hi> which, instead of protecting, they had made a prey of." Note, Those that are enriching themselves with the spoils of the public cannot expect that they shall always be suffered to do so. Nor will God always permit his people to be trampled upon by those that should support them, but will find a time to deliver them from the shepherds their false friends, as well as from the lions their open enemies. <div eID="gen19085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19086" type="x-p"/> II. How much concerned God is for the flock; he speaks as if he were the more concerned for them because he saw them thus neglected, for <hi type="italic">with him the fatherless finds mercy.</hi> Precious promises are made here upon the occasion, which were to have their accomplishment in the return of the Jews out of their captivity and their re-establishment in their own land. Let the shepherds <hi type="italic">hear this word of the Lord,</hi> and know that they have no part nor lot in the matter. But let the poor sheep hear it and take the comfort of it. Note, Though magistrates and ministers fail in doing their part, for the good of the church, yet God will not fail in doing his; he will take the flock into his own hand rather than the church shall come short of any kindness he has designed for it. The under-shepherds may prove careless, but the chief Shepherd <hi type="italic">neither slumbers nor sleeps.</hi> They may be false, but God <hi type="italic">abides faithful.</hi> <div eID="gen19086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19087" type="x-p"/> 1. God will gather his sheep together that were scattered, and bring those back to the fold that had wandered from it: "<hi type="italic">I, even I,</hi> who alone can do it, will do it, and will have all the glory of it. <hi type="italic">I will both search my sheep and find them out</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.11">v. 11</reference>) as a <hi type="italic">shepherd</hi> does (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.12">v. 12</reference>), and bring them back as he does the stray-sheep, upon his shoulders, <hi type="italic">from all the places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day.</hi>" There are cloudy and dark days, windy and stormy ones, which scatter God's sheep, which send them hither and thither, to divers and distant places, in quest of secresy and safety. But, (1.) Wherever they are the eye of God will <hi type="italic">find them out;</hi> for his eyes run to and fro through the earth, in favour of them. <hi type="italic">I will seek out my sheep;</hi> and not one that belongs to the fold, though driven ever so far off, shall be lost. <hi type="italic">The Lord knows those that are his;</hi> he <hi type="italic">knows their work</hi> and <hi type="italic">where they dwell</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.13">Rev. ii. 13</reference>), and where they are hidden. (2.) When his time shall come his arms will <hi type="italic">fetch them home</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will bring them out from the people.</hi> God will both incline their hearts to come by his grace and will by his providence open a door for them and remove every difficulty that lies in the way. They shall not return one by one, clandestinely stealing away, but they shall return in a body: "<hi type="italic">I will gather them from the countries</hi> into which they are dispersed, not only the most considerable families of them, but every particular person. <hi type="italic">I will seek that which was lost and bring again that which was driven away,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.16">v. 16</reference>. This was done when so many thousand Jews returned triumphantly out of Babylon, under the conduct of Zerubbabel, Ezra, and others. When those that have gone astray from God into the paths of sin are brought back by repentance, when those that erred come to the acknowledgment of the truth, when God's outcasts are gathered and restored, and religious assemblies, that were dispersed, rally again, upon the ceasing of persecution, and when the churches have rest and liberty, then this promise has a further accomplishment. <div eID="gen19087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19088" type="x-p"/> 2. God will feed his people as the <hi type="italic">sheep of his pasture,</hi> that had been famished. God will bring the returning captives safely to their own land (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.13">v. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">will feed them upon the mountains of Israel,</hi> and that is a <hi type="italic">good pasture,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">fat pasture</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.14">v. 14</reference>); there shall their <hi type="italic">feeding</hi> be, and there shall be <hi type="italic">their fold;</hi> and it is a <hi type="italic">good fold.</hi> There God will not only <hi type="italic">feed them,</hi> but <hi type="italic">cause them to lie down</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.15">v. 15</reference>), which denotes a comfortable rest after they had tired themselves with their wanderings, and a constant continuing residence; they shall not be driven out again from these green pastures, as they have been, nor shall they be disturbed, but shall lie down in a sweet repose and there shall be <hi type="italic">none to make them afraid.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.23.2">Ps. xxiii. 2</reference>, <hi type="italic">He makes me to lie down in green pastures.</hi> Compare this with the like promise (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.3-Jer.23.4">Jer. xxiii. 3, 4</reference>), when God restored them not only to the milk and honey of their own land, to the enjoyment of its fruits, but to the privileges of his sanctuary on Mount Zion, the chief of the mountains of Israel. When they had an altar and a temple again, and the benefit of a settled priesthood, then they were fed in a good pasture. <div eID="gen19088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19089" type="x-p"/> 3. He will succour those that are hurt, will <hi type="italic">bind up that which was broken and strengthen that which was sick,</hi> will comfort those that <hi type="italic">mourn in Zion</hi> and with Zion. If ministers, who should speak peace to those who are of a sorrowful spirit, neglect their duty, yet the Holy Ghost the Comforter will be faithful to his office. But, as it follows, the <hi type="italic">fat and the strong shall be destroyed.</hi> He that has rest for disquieted saints has terror to speak to presumptuous sinners. As <hi type="italic">every valley</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">filled,</hi> so <hi type="italic">every mountain and hill shall be brought low,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.3.5">Luke iii. 5</reference>.
entries.9d526e11762b25416befee86ffb2ffefa7b0b1b5: <div eID="gen19089" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Care of His Flock; Prediction of Messiah's Kingdom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19090" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And <hi type="italic">as for</hi> you, O my flock, thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I judge between cattle and cattle, between the rams and the he goats. <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">Seemeth it</hi> a small thing unto you to have eaten up the good pasture, but ye must tread down with your feet the residue of your pastures? and to have drunk of the deep waters, but ye must foul the residue with your feet? <hi type="super">19</hi> And <hi type="italic">as for</hi> my flock, they eat that which ye have trodden with your feet; and they drink that which ye have fouled with your feet. <hi type="super">20</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> unto them; Behold, I, <hi type="italic">even</hi> I, will judge between the fat cattle and between the lean cattle. <hi type="super">21</hi> Because ye have thrust with side and with shoulder, and pushed all the diseased with your horns, till ye have scattered them abroad; <hi type="super">22</hi> Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle. <hi type="super">23</hi> And I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. <hi type="super">24</hi> And I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will be their God, and my servant David a prince among them; I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">25</hi> And I will make with them a covenant of peace, and will cause the evil beasts to cease out of the land: and they shall dwell safely in the wilderness, and sleep in the woods. <hi type="super">26</hi> And I will make them and the places round about my hill a blessing; and I will cause the shower to come down in his season; there shall be showers of blessing. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the tree of the field shall yield her fruit, and the earth shall yield her increase, and they shall be safe in their land, and shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , when I have broken the bands of their yoke, and delivered them out of the hand of those that served themselves of them. <hi type="super">28</hi> And they shall no more be a prey to the heathen, neither shall the beast of the land devour them; but they shall dwell safely, and none shall make <hi type="italic">them</hi> afraid. <hi type="super">29</hi> And I will raise up for them a plant of renown, and they shall be no more consumed with hunger in the land, neither bear the shame of the heathen any more. <hi type="super">30</hi> Thus shall they know that I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God <hi type="italic">am</hi> with them, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> they, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the house of Israel, <hi type="italic">are</hi> my people, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">31</hi> And ye my flock, the flock of my pasture, <hi type="italic">are</hi> men, <hi type="italic">and</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> your God, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen19090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19091" type="x-p"/> The prophet has no more to say to the shepherds, but he has now a message to deliver to the flock. God had ordered him to speak tenderly to them, and to assure them of the mercy he had in store for them. But here he is ordered to make a difference between some and others of them, to separate between the precious and the vile and then to give them a promise of the Messiah, by whom this distinction should be effectually made, partly at his first coming (for <hi type="italic">for judgment he came into this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.9.39">John ix. 39</reference>, to <hi type="italic">fill the hungry with good things and to send the rich empty away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.53">Luke i. 53</reference>), but completely at his second coming, when he shall, as it is here said, <hi type="italic">judge between cattle and cattle, as a shepherd divides between the sheep and the goats, and shall set the sheep on his right hand and the goats on his left</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.32-Matt.25.33">Matt. xxv. 32, 33</reference>), which seems to have reference to this. We have here, <div eID="gen19091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19092" type="x-p"/> I. Conviction spoken to those of the flock that were fat and strong, the <hi type="italic">rams and the he-goats</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.17">v. 17</reference>), those that, though they had not power, as shepherds and rulers, to oppress with, yet, being rich and wealthy, made use of the opportunity which this gave them to bear hard upon their poor neighbours. Those that have much would have more, and, if they set to it, will have more, so many ways have they of encroaching upon their poor neighbours, and forcing from them the one ewe-lamb, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.4">2 Sam. xii. 4</reference>. Do not the rich oppress the poor merely with the help of their riches, and <hi type="italic">draw them before the judgment-seats?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.6">Jam. ii. 6</reference>. Poor servants and tenants are hardly used by their rich lords and masters. The <hi type="italic">rams</hi> and the <hi type="italic">he-goats</hi> not only kept all the good pasture to themselves, ate the fat and drank the sweet, but they would not let the poor of the flock have any comfortable enjoyment of the little that was left them; they <hi type="italic">trod down the residue of the pastures and fouled the residue of the waters,</hi> so that the flock was obliged to eat that which they had trodden into the dirt, and drink that which they had muddied, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.18-Ezek.34.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. This intimates that the great men not only by extortion and oppression made and kept their neighbours poor, and scarcely left them enough to subsist on, but were so vexatious to them that what little coarse fare they had was embittered to them. And this <hi type="italic">seemed a small thing</hi> to them; they thought there was no harm in it, as if it were the privilege of their quality to be injurious to all their neighbours. Note, Many that live in pomp and at ease themselves care not what straits those about them are reduced to, so they may but have every thing to their mind. Those that <hi type="italic">are at ease,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the proud,</hi> grudge that any body should live by them with any comfort. But this as not all; they not only robbed the poor, to make them poorer, but were troublesome to the sick and weak of the flock (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.21">v. 21</reference>): They <hi type="italic">thrust with side and shoulder</hi> those that were feeble (for the weakest goes to the wall) and <hi type="italic">pushed the diseased with their horns,</hi> because they knew they could be too hard for them, when they durst not meddle with their match. It has been observed concerning sheep that if one of the flock be sick and faint the rest will secure it as well as they can, and shelter it from the scorching heat of the sun; but these, on the contrary, were most injurious to the diseased. Those that they could not serve themselves of they did what they could to rid the country of, and so <hi type="italic">scattered them abroad,</hi> as if the poor, whom, Christ says, we must have always with us, were public nuisances, not to be relieved, but sent far away from us. Note, It is a barbarous thing to <hi type="italic">add affliction to the afflicted.</hi> Perhaps these <hi type="italic">rams</hi> and <hi type="italic">he-goats</hi> are designed to represent the scribes and Pharisees, for they are such troublers of the church as Christ himself must come to deliver it from, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">v. 23</reference>. They devoured widows' houses, took away the key of knowledge, corrupted the pure water of divine truths, and oppressed the consciences of men with the traditions of the elders, besides that they were continually vexatious and injurious to <hi type="italic">the poor of the flock</hi> that <hi type="italic">waited on the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.11.11">Zech. xi. 11</reference>. Note, It is no new thing for the flock of God to receive a great deal of damage and mischief from those that are themselves of the flock, and in eminent stations in it, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.30">Acts xx. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen19092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19093" type="x-p"/> II. Comfort spoken to those of the flock that are poor and feeble, and that wait for the consolation of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will save my flock,</hi> and they shall no more be spoiled as they have been by the beasts of prey, by their own shepherds or by the rams and he-goats among themselves." Upon this occasion, as is usual in the prophets, comes in a prediction of the coming of the Messiah, and the setting up of his kingdom, and the exceedingly great and precious benefits which the church should enjoy under the protection and influence of that kingdom. Observe what is here foretold, <div eID="gen19093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19094" type="x-p"/> 1. Concerning the Messiah himself. (1.) He shall have his commission from God himself: I will <hi type="italic">set him up</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">v. 23</reference>); <hi type="italic">I will raise him up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.29">v. 29</reference>. He sanctified and sealed him, appointed and anointed him. (2.) He shall be the great <hi type="italic">Shepherd</hi> of the sheep, who shall do that for his flock which no one else could do. He is the <hi type="italic">one Shepherd,</hi> under whom Jews and Gentiles should be <hi type="italic">one fold.</hi> (3.) He is <hi type="italic">God's servant,</hi> employed by him and for him, and doing all in obedience to his will, with an eye to his glory—his servant, to re-establish his kingdom among men and advance the interests of that kingdom. (4.) He is David, one after God's own heart, set as his King upon the holy hill of Zion, made the head of the corner, with whom the covenant of royalty is made, and to whom God would <hi type="italic">give the throne of his father David.</hi> He is both the <hi type="italic">root and offspring of David.</hi> (5.) He is the <hi type="italic">plant of renown,</hi> because a <hi type="italic">righteous branch</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer. xxiii. 5</reference>), a branch of the Lord, that is <hi type="italic">beautiful</hi> and <hi type="italic">glorious,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Isa. iv. 2</reference>. He has a name above every name, a throne above every throne, and may therefore well be called a <hi type="italic">branch of renown.</hi> Some understand it of the church, the <hi type="italic">planting of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa. lxi. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Its name shall be remembered</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.17">Ps. xlv. 17</reference>) and Christ's in it. <div eID="gen19094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19095" type="x-p"/> 2. Concerning the great charter by which the kingdom of the Messiah should be incorporated, and upon which it should be founded (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will make with them a covenant of peace.</hi> The covenant of grace is a covenant of peace. In it God is at peace with us, speaks peace to us, and assures us of peace, of all good, all the good we need to make us happy. The tenour of this covenant is: "<hi type="italic">I the Lord will be their God,</hi> a God all-sufficient to them (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">v. 24</reference>), will own them and will be owned by them; in order to this <hi type="italic">my servant David shall be a prince among them,</hi> to reduce them to their allegiance, to receive their homage, and to reign over them, in them, and for them." Note, Those, and those only, that have the Lord Jesus for <hi type="italic">their prince</hi> have the Lord Jehovah for <hi type="italic">their God.</hi> And then <hi type="italic">they, even the house of Israel, shall be my people.</hi> If we take God to be <hi type="italic">our God,</hi> he will take us to be <hi type="italic">his people.</hi> From this covenant between God and Israel there results communion: "<hi type="italic">I the Lord their God am with them,</hi> to converse with them; and <hi type="italic">they shall know it,</hi> and have the comfort of it." <div eID="gen19095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19096" type="x-p"/> 3. Concerning the privileges of those that are the faithful subjects of this kingdom of the Messiah and interested in the covenant of peace. These are here set forth figuratively, as the blessings of the flock. But we have a key to it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.31">v. 31</reference>. Those that belong to this flock, though they are spoken of as <hi type="italic">sheep,</hi> are really men, men that have <hi type="italic">the Lord for their God,</hi> and are in covenant with him. Now to them it is promised, <div eID="gen19096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19097" type="x-p"/> (1.) That they shall enjoy a holy security under the divine protection. Christ, our good Shepherd, has <hi type="italic">caused the evil beasts to cease out of the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.25">v. 25</reference>), having vanquished all our spiritual enemies, broken their power, and triumphed over them; the roaring lion is not a roaring devouring lion to them; <hi type="italic">they shall no more be a prey to the heathen</hi> nor the heathen a terror to them, <hi type="italic">neither shall the beasts of the land devour them.</hi> Sin and Satan, death and hell, are conquered. And then <hi type="italic">they shall dwell safely,</hi> not only in the folds, but in the fields, <hi type="italic">in the wilderness, in the woods,</hi> where the beasts of prey are; they shall not only dwell there, but they shall sleep there, which denotes not only that the beasts being <hi type="italic">made to cease</hi> there shall be no danger, but, their consciences being purified and pacified, they shall be in no apprehension of danger; not only safe from evil, but quiet from the fear of evil. Note, Those may lay down and sleep securely, sleep at ease, that have Christ for their prince; for he will be their protector, and make them to dwell in safety. None shall hurt them, nay, <hi type="italic">none shall make them afraid.</hi> If God be for us, who can be against us? <hi type="italic">Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed.</hi> Through Christ, God delivers his people not only from the things they have reason to fear, but from their fear even of death itself, from all that fear that has torment. This safety from evil is promised (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall be safe in their land,</hi> in no danger of being invaded and enslaved, though their great plenty be a temptation to their neighbours to <hi type="italic">desire their land;</hi> and that which shall make them think themselves safe is their confidence in the wisdom, power, and goodness of God: <hi type="italic">They shall know that I am the Lord.</hi> All our disquieting fears arise from our ignorance of God and mistakes concerning him. Their experience of his particular care concerning them encourages their confidence in him: "<hi type="italic">I have broken the bands of their yoke,</hi> with which they have been brought and held down under oppression, and have <hi type="italic">delivered them out of the hand of those that served themselves of them,</hi> whence they shall argue, He that has delivered does and will, therefore will we dwell safely." This is explained, and applied to our gospel-state, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.74">Luke i. 74</reference>. <hi type="italic">That we, being delivered out of the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear,</hi> as those may do that serve him in faith. <div eID="gen19097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19098" type="x-p"/> (2.) That they shall enjoy a spiritual plenty of all good things, the best things, for their comfort and happiness: <hi type="italic">They shall no more be consumed with hunger in the land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.29">v. 29</reference>. Famine and scarcity, when Israel was punished with that judgment, turned as much to their reproach among the heathen as any other, because the fruitfulness of Canaan was so much talked of. But now <hi type="italic">they shall not bear that shame of the heathen any more</hi> For the <hi type="italic">showers shall come down in their season,</hi> even <hi type="italic">showers of blessing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.26">v. 26</reference>. Christ is a Shepherd that will feed his people; and they shall <hi type="italic">go in and out, and find pasture.</hi> [1.] They shall not be consumed with hunger; for they shall not be put off with the world for a portion, which is not bread, which satisfies not, and which leaves those that are put off with it to be <hi type="italic">consumed with hunger.</hi> The ordinances of the ceremonial law are called <hi type="italic">beggarly elements,</hi> for there was little in them, compared with the Christian institutes, <hi type="italic">wherewith the mower fills his hand and he that binds sheaves his bosom.</hi> Those that <hi type="italic">hunger and thirst after righteousness</hi> shall not be consumed with that hunger, for <hi type="italic">they shall be filled.</hi> And he that drinks of the water that Christ gives him, the still waters by which he leads his sheep, shall <hi type="italic">never thirst.</hi> [2.] <hi type="italic">Showers of blessings</hi> shall come upon them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.26-Ezek.34.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. The heavens shall yield their dews; the <hi type="italic">trees of the field</hi> also shall <hi type="italic">yield their fruit.</hi> The seat of this plenty is <hi type="italic">God's hill,</hi> his holy hill of Zion, for on that mountain, in the gospel church, it is, that God has <hi type="italic">made to all nations a feast;</hi> to that those must join themselves who would partake of gospel benefits. The cause of this plenty is the <hi type="italic">showers that come down in their season,</hi> that descend upon the mountains of Zion, the graces of Christ, his doctrine that drops as the dew, the graces of Christ, and the fruits and comforts of his Spirit, by which we are made fruitful in the fruits of righteousness. The instances of this plenty are the blessings of heaven poured down upon us and the productions of grace brought forth by us, our comfort in God's favour and God's glory in our fruit-bearing. The extent of this plenty is very large, to all the <hi type="italic">places round about my hill;</hi> for <hi type="italic">out of Zion shall go forth the law,</hi> shall go forth light to a dark world, and the river that shall water a dry and desert world; all that are in the neighbourhood of Zion shall fare the better for it; and the nearer the church the nearer its God. And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">effect of this plenty</hi> is, <hi type="italic">I will make them a blessing,</hi> eminently and exemplarily blessed, patterns of happiness, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.24">Isa. xix. 24</reference>. Or, They shall be blessings to all about them, diffusively useful. Note, Those that are the <hi type="italic">blessed of the Lord</hi> must study to make themselves blessings to the world. He that is good, let him do <hi type="italic">good;</hi> he that has received the gift, the grace, let him minister the same. <div eID="gen19098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19099" type="x-p"/> Now this promise of the Messiah and his kingdom spoke much comfort to those to whom it was then made, for they might be sure that God would not utterly <hi type="italic">destroy</hi> their nation, how low soever it might be brought, as long as that <hi type="italic">blessing</hi> was <hi type="italic">in</hi> the womb of <hi type="italic">it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.8">Isa. lxv. 8</reference>. But it speaks much more comfort to us, to whom it is fulfilled, who are the sheep of this good Shepherd, are fed in his pastures, and <hi type="italic">blessed with all spiritual blessings in heavenly things</hi> by him.  <chapter eID="Ezek.34"/> <div eID="gen19099" type="x-p"/>

entries.e3dc7c57a481894cafc390145e6fae47501b735a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11677"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 34</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.34.1-Ezek.34.31">Eze 34:1-31</reference>. Reproof of the False Shepherds; Promise of the True and Good Shepherd.</title> <div sID="gen21153" type="x-p"/> Having in the thirty-third chapter laid down repentance as the necessary preliminary to happier times for the people, He now promises the removal of the false shepherds as preparatory to the raising up of the Good Shepherd.<div eID="gen21153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11677"/>2. <reference osisRef="Jer.23.1">Jr 23:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Zech.11.17">Zec 11:17</reference> similarly make the removal of the false shepherds the preliminary to the interposition of Messiah the Good Shepherd in behalf of His people Israel. The "shepherds" are not prophets or priests, but rulers who sought in their government their own selfish ends, not the good of the people ruled. The term was appropriate, as David, the first king and the type of the true David (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">24</reference>), was taken from being a shepherd (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.2">2Sa 5:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.70">Psa 78:70</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.71">71</reference>); and the office, like that of a shepherd for his flock, is to guard and provide for his people. The choice of a shepherd for the first king was therefore designed to suggest this thought, just as Jesus' selection of fishermen for apostles was designed to remind them of their spiritual office of catching men (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Is 44:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.8">Jr 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.15">3:15</reference>; 10:21; 23:1, 2). <div eID="gen21154" type="x-p"/>
entries.9bea108bb136a70ccf11dcefc6a76a2adecd1f0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11678"/><div sID="gen21155" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11678"/><hi type="bold">3. fat--</hi>or, by differently pointing the Hebrew, "milk" [Septuagint]. Thus the repetition "fat" and "fed" is avoided: also the eating of "fat" would not probably be put before the "killing" of the sheep. The eating of sheep's or goats' milk as food (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.14">De 32:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.27.27">Pr 27:27</reference>) was unobjectionable, had not these shepherds milked them too often, and that without duly "feeding" them [Bochart], (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">Is 56:11</reference>). The rulers levied exorbitant tributes.<div eID="gen21155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kill ... fed--</hi>kill the rich by false accusation so as to get possession of their property.<div eID="gen21156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feed not ... flock--</hi>take no care of the people (<reference osisRef="John.10.12">Joh 10:12</reference>). <div eID="gen21157" type="x-p"/>
entries.652e291f0d4c48d51cf4e57a1a3c2ebaecf9663d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11679"/><div sID="gen21158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11679"/><hi type="bold">4. The diseased--</hi>rather, those weak from the effects of "disease," as "strengthened" (that is, with due nourishment) requires [Grotius].<div eID="gen21158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">broken--</hi>that is, fractures from wounds inflicted by the wolf.<div eID="gen21159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought again ... driven away--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.23.4">Ex 23:4</reference>). Those "driven away" by the enemy into foreign lands through God's judgments are meant (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.3">Jr 23:3</reference>). A spiritual reformation of the state by the rulers would have turned away God's wrath, and "brought again" the exiles. The rulers are censured as chiefly guilty (though the people, too, were guilty), because they, who ought to have been foremost in checking the evil, promoted it.<div eID="gen21160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither ... sought ... lost--</hi>Contrast the Good Shepherd's love (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.4">Lu 15:4</reference>).<div eID="gen21161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with force ... ruled--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.1.13">Ex 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.14">14</reference>). With an Egyptian bondage. The very thing forbidden by the law they did (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.43">Le 25:43</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.3">1Pe 5:3</reference>). <div eID="gen21162" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d35833c9c17dd859cf816b25a76f144e6fb2027: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11680"/><div sID="gen21163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11680"/><hi type="bold">5. scattered, because ... no shepherd--</hi>that is, none worthy of the name, though there were some called shepherds (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.17">1Ki 22:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.36">Mt 9:36</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.26.31">Mt 26:31</reference>, where the sheep were scattered when the true Shepherd was smitten. God calls them "My sheep"; for they were not, as the shepherds treated them, their patrimony whereby to "feed themselves."<div eID="gen21163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">meat to all ... beasts--</hi>They became a prey to the Syrians, Ammon, Moab, and Assyria. <div eID="gen21164" type="x-p"/>
entries.96a1cb158d11b19bc3e3f61a60fab82473e57098: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11681"/><div sID="gen21165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11681"/><hi type="bold">6. every high hill--</hi>the scene of their idolatries sanctioned by the rulers.<div eID="gen21165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">search ... seek--</hi>rather, "seek ... search." The former is the part of the superior rulers to inquire after: to search out is the duty of the subordinate rulers [Junius]. <div eID="gen21166" type="x-p"/>
entries.870d010a9bf9c779b3ead6c825ff24b420d0bbf7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11682"/><div sID="gen21167" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11682"/><hi type="bold">10. I will require my flock--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">He 13:17</reference>), rather, "I require," &c., for God already had begun to do so, punishing Zedekiah and the other princes severely (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.10">Jr 52:10</reference>). <div eID="gen21167" type="x-p"/>
entries.e15a9b53100fae2d6a463c67473145867fc179ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11683"/><div sID="gen21168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11683"/><hi type="bold">11. I ... will ... search--</hi>doing that which the so-called shepherds had failed to do, I being the rightful owner of the flock. <div eID="gen21168" type="x-p"/>
entries.63cdc365c405e8d7f7d8420009f349943b46563c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11684"/><div sID="gen21169" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11684"/><hi type="bold">12. in the day that he is among--</hi>in the midst of (Hebrew) His sheep that had been scattered. Referring to Messiah's second advent, when He shall be "the glory in the midst of Israel" (<reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zec 2:5</reference>).<div eID="gen21169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the cloudy ... day--</hi>the day of the nation's calamity (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.2">Joe 2:2</reference>). <div eID="gen21170" type="x-p"/>
entries.8735dd0780d9aab01e500e702bbc7ecc4c25c351: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11685"/><div sID="gen21171" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11685"/><hi type="bold">13. And I will bring them out from the people, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.25">Eze 28:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.24">36:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.21">37:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.9">Is 65:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.3">Jr 23:3</reference>). <div eID="gen21171" type="x-p"/>
entries.273bdc280057fba34278259cd4f0f0c9d8932fc0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11686"/><div sID="gen21172" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11686"/><hi type="bold">14. good pasture--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.23.2">Psa 23:2</reference>).<div eID="gen21172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">high mountains of Israel--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.23">Eze 17:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.40">20:40</reference>, the phrase is "the mountain of the height of Israel" in the singular number. The reason for the difference is: there Ezekiel spoke of the central seat of the kingdom, Mount Zion, where the people met for the worship of Jehovah; here he speaks of the kingdom of Israel at large, all the parts of which are regarded as possessing a moral elevation. <div eID="gen21173" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c149bbbef708276674c660627ba48b06afd48ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11687"/><div sID="gen21174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11687"/>16. In contrast to the unfaithful shepherds (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.4">Eze 34:4</reference>). The several duties neglected by them I will faithfully discharge.<div eID="gen21174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fat ... strong--</hi>that is, those rendered wanton by prosperity (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">De 32:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.28">Jr 5:28</reference>), who use their strength to oppress the weak. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.20">Eze 34:20</reference>, "the fat cattle" (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.16">Is 10:16</reference>). The image is from fat cattle that wax refractory.<div eID="gen21175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with judgment--</hi>that is, justice and equity, as contrasted with the "force" and "cruelty" with which the unfaithful shepherds ruled the flock (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.4">Eze 34:4</reference>). <div eID="gen21176" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a5f763dc1604ba47b3ce036edfd95b5b58ed78b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11688"/><div sID="gen21177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11688"/><hi type="bold">17. you, ... my flock--</hi>passing from the rulers to the people.<div eID="gen21177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cattle and cattle--</hi>rather, "sheep and sheep"; Margin, "small cattle," or "flocks of lambs and kids," that is, I judge between one class of citizens and another, so as to award what is right to each. He then defines the class about to be punitively "judged," namely, "the rams and he-goats," or "great he-goats" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Is 14:9</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.3">Zec 10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.32">Mt 25:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.33">33</reference>). They answer to "the fat and strong," as opposed to the "sick" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.16">Eze 34:16</reference>). The rich and ungodly of the people are meant, who imitated the bad rulers in oppressing their poorer brethren, as if it enhanced their own joys to trample on others' rights (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.18">Eze 34:18</reference>). <div eID="gen21178" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7addd152326211929488a9ddcdc014bdfea7dce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11689"/><div sID="gen21179" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11689"/>18-19. Not content with appropriating to their own use the goods of others, they from mere wantonness spoiled what they did not use, so as to be of no use to the owners.<div eID="gen21179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21180" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deep waters--</hi>that is, "limpid," as deep waters are generally clear. Grotius explains the image as referring to the usuries with which the rich ground the poor (<reference osisRef="Ezek.22.12">Eze 22:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.2">Is 24:2</reference>). <div eID="gen21180" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee57585facd0b18e4c5a31fd900b250ed64f83e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11691"/><div sID="gen21183" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11691"/><hi type="bold">20. fat ... lean--</hi>the rich oppressors ... the humble poor. <div eID="gen21183" type="x-p"/>
entries.85add575eba1675dec93df11bd9dede614f435b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11692"/><div sID="gen21184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11692"/><hi type="bold">21. scattered them abroad--</hi>down to the time of the carrying away to Babylon [Grotius]. <div eID="gen21184" type="x-p"/>
entries.2beb05f27bf93c5cc543799229ff52769e49264e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11693"/><div sID="gen21185" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11693"/>22. After the restoration from Babylon, the Jews were delivered in some degree from the oppression, not only of foreigners, but also of their own great people (<reference osisRef="Neh.5.1-Neh.5.19">Ne 5:1-19</reference>). The full and final fulfilment of this prophecy is future. <div eID="gen21185" type="x-p"/>
entries.55cd04d28e627a4b88b3729fd69b79c3f7d08444: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11694"/><div sID="gen21186" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11694"/><hi type="bold">23. set up--</hi>that is, raise up by divine appointment; alluding to the declaration of God to David, "I will set up thy seed after thee" (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.12">2Sa 7:12</reference>); and, "Yet have I set My king on My holy hill of Zion" (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>; 13:23).<div eID="gen21186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one shepherd--</hi>literally, "a Shepherd, one": singularly and pre-eminently one: the only one of His kind, to whom none is comparable (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>). The Lord Jesus refers to this prophecy (<reference osisRef="John.10.14">Joh 10:14</reference>), "I am THE Good Shepherd." Also "one" as uniting in one the heretofore divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah, and also "gathering together in one all things in Christ, both which are in heaven and on earth" (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>); thus healing worse breaches than that between Israel and Judah (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>). "God by Him reconciling all things unto Himself, whether things in earth or in heaven."<div eID="gen21187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">David--</hi>the antitypical David, Messiah, of the seed of David, which no other king after the captivity was: who was fully, what David was only in a degree, "the man after God's own heart." Also, David means beloved: Messiah was truly God's beloved Son (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>). Shepherd means King, rather than religious instructor; in this pre-eminently He was the true David, who was the Shepherd King (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Lu 1:32</reference>, 33). Messiah is called "David" in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Is 55:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jr 30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>. <div eID="gen21188" type="x-p"/>
entries.45f3e92ebf93f9298fbd07599e4b37a14ac8d8e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11695"/><div sID="gen21189" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11695"/><hi type="bold">24. my servant--</hi>implying fitness for ruling in the name of God, not pursuing a self-chosen course, as other kings, but acting as the faithful administrator of the will of God; Messiah realized fully this character (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.40.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.3">49:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">53:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.7">Php 2:7</reference>), which David typically and partially represented (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.36">Ac 13:36</reference>); so He is the fittest person to wield the world scepter, abused by all the world kings (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.34">Da 2:34</reference>, 35, 44, 45). <div eID="gen21189" type="x-p"/>
entries.267915c27cc848f2bef88a29ec2266ddb093b936: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11696"/><div sID="gen21190" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11696"/><hi type="bold">25. covenant of peace ... evil beasts ... to cease ... dwell safely--</hi>The original promise of the law (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.6">Le 26:6</reference>) shall be realized for the first time fully under Messiah (Is 11:6-9; 35:<reference osisRef="Isa.9.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Ho 2:18</reference>). <div eID="gen21190" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e624e2dda01e8f53e5dbe94671780cf7846f4f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11697"/><div sID="gen21191" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11697"/><hi type="bold">26. them and the places round about my hill--</hi>The Jews, and Zion, God's hill (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>), are to be sources of blessing, not merely to themselves, but to the surrounding heathen (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.24">Is 19:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.56.6">56:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.3">60:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mi 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.13">Zec 8:13</reference>). The literal fulfilment is, however, the primary one, though the spiritual also is designed. In correspondence with the settled reign of righteousness internally, all is to be prosperity externally, fertilizing showers (according to the promise of the ancient covenant, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.4">Le 26:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.9">Psa 68:9</reference>; Mal 3:10), and productive trees and lands (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.27">Eze 34:27</reference>). Thus shall they realize the image of <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.14">Eze 34:14</reference>; namely, a flock richly pastured by God Himself. <div eID="gen21191" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3cc9945af3d1dabde2bc9a4ebebe7721f6a5bfc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11698"/><div sID="gen21192" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11698"/><hi type="bold">27. served themselves of them--</hi>availed themselves of their services, as if the Jews were their slaves (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13">Jr 22:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.14">25:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.15.13">Ge 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.1.14">Ex 1:14</reference>). <div eID="gen21192" type="x-p"/>
entries.443d355107d8a3ba952debdbe10e99abfa36b66e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11699"/><div sID="gen21193" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11699"/><hi type="bold">28. dwell safely--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>). <div eID="gen21193" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0085dce58d68f80dcdbc9afe6b92e64a64cefa8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11700"/><div sID="gen21194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11700"/><hi type="bold">29. plant of renown--</hi>Messiah, the "Rod" and "Branch" (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Is 11:1</reference>), the "righteous Branch" (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>), who shall obtain for them "renown." Fairbairn less probably translates, "A plantation for a name," that is, a flourishing condition, represented as a garden (alluding to Eden, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.8-Gen.2.11">Ge 2:8-11</reference>, with its various trees, good for food and pleasant to the sight), the planting of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">Is 60:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">61:3</reference>), and an object of "renown" among the heathen. <div eID="gen21194" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9aff95fbbd0069639e5327f974bd97fe63dd6e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11701"/><div sID="gen21195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11701"/><hi type="bold">31. ye my flock ... are men--</hi>not merely an explanation of the image, as Jerome represents. But as God had promised many things which mere "men" could not expect to realize, He shows that it is not from man's might their realization is to be looked for, but from God, who would perform them for His covenant-people, "His flock" [Rosenmuller]. When we realize most our weakness and God's power and faithfulness to His covenant, we are in the fittest state for receiving His blessings. <chapter eID="Ezek.34"/>

entries.d2fd7c49a8fd7b3cc4a6390f2f499411d879e7b3: <div eID="gen32258" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32259" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32260" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32260" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32259" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32261" type="x-p"/> The prophet is commanded to declare the dreadful judgments of God against the covetous shepherds of Israel, who feed themselves, and not their flocks; by which emblem the priests and Levites are intended, who in Ezekiel's time were very corrupt, and the chief cause of Israel's apostasy and ruin, <reference osisRef="Eze.34.1-Eze.34.10">Eze 34:1-10</reference>. From this gloomy subject the prophet passes to the blessedness of the true Israel of God under the reign of David, the Great Shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ being named after this prince by a figure exceedingly frequent in the sacred oracles, of putting the type for the antitype, vv. 11-31.
entries.2ca842231bdc11ceea6087b4f5605a1539eb0c11: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32262" type="x-p"/> Prophesy against the shepherds of Israel - The shepherds include, first, the priests and Levites; secondly, the kings, princes, and magistrates. The flock means the whole of the people. The fat and the wool, the tithes and offerings, the taxes and imposts. The reprehensible feeding and clothing with these, as to the priests and Levites, the using these tithes and offerings, not to enable them the better to fulfill the work of the ministry, but to pamper their own bodies, and support them in an idle voluptuous life; and in reference to the state, the employing the taxes and imposts, not for the support and administration of justice and good government, but to subsidize heathen powers, and maintain their own luxury and idolatrous prodigality.
entries.48c2624500587461ea1cfce5d95126d4d84fc7e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen32262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32263" type="x-p"/> Ye eat the fat - I think החלב hacheleb should be translated the milk, and so most of the Versions understand it. Or they lived on the fat sheep, and took the wool of all. "The priests," says Calmet, "ate the tithes, the first-fruits, and the offerings of the people; the princes received the tributes and imposts and instead of instructing and protecting them, the latter took away their lives by the cruelties they practiced against them: the former destroyed their souls by the poison of their doctrine, and by their bad example. The fat sheep point out the rich to whom these pastors often disguised the truth, by a cruel condescension and complaisance."
entries.433b3d3bdba6e467b92519310dff49791fdc33e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen32263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32264" type="x-p"/> The diseased have ye not strengthened - No person is fit for the office of a shepherd, who does not well understand the diseases to which sheep are incident, and the mode of cure. And is any man fit for the pastoral office, or to be a shepherd of souls, who is not well acquainted with the disease of sin in all its varieties, and the remedy for this disease, and the proper mode of administering it, in those various cases? He who does not know Jesus Christ as his own Savior, never can recommend him to others. He who is not saved, will not save. <div eID="gen32264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32265" type="x-p"/> Neither have ye healed that which was sick - The prophet first speaks of the general disease; next, of the different kinds of spiritual infirmity. <div eID="gen32265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32266" type="x-p"/> Neither have ye bound up that which was broken - If a sheep have broken a leg, a proper shepherd knows how to set the bones, and splint and bind it till the bones knit and become strong. And the skillful spiritual pastor knows, if one of the flock be overtaken in a fault, how to restore such. Those sudden falls, where there was not a strong propensity to sin, are, to the soul, as a broken bone to the body. <div eID="gen32266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32267" type="x-p"/> Neither have ye brought again - A proper shepherd loves his sheep: he feels interested for their welfare; he acquaints himself with them all, so that he knows and can distinguish each. He knows also their number, and frequently counts to see that none is missing; if one be lost or strayed, he goes immediately and seeks it; and as he is constantly on the watch, it cannot have strayed far before he is apprised of its absence from the flock; and the less it has strayed, the sooner it is found and brought back to the fold. <div eID="gen32267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32268" type="x-p"/> The shepherds of Israel knew nothing about their flock; they might have been diseased, infirm, bruised, maimed, their limbs broken, strayed, and lost; for they watched not over them. When they got fat sheep and wool for their table and their clothing, they regarded nothing else; as they considered the flock given them for their own use, and scarcely ever supposed that they were to give any thing in return for the milk and the wool. <div eID="gen32268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32269" type="x-p"/> But with force and with cruelty - Exacting tithes and dues by the strong arm of the law, with the most ungodly feeling; and with a cruelty of disposition that proved it was the fat and the wool they sought, and not the safety or comfort of the flock.
entries.5a748b645c4ae52e0764b06aa6ee370dd50522b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32270" type="x-p"/> And they were scattered - There was no discipline kept up; and the flock, the Church, became disorganized, and separated from each other, both in affection and fellowship. And the consequence was, the grievous wolves, false and worldly interested teachers, seized on and made a prey of them. Of the communion of saints such shepherds know nothing, farther than that it makes a part of the common creed.
entries.f7f5bf6a80b125018821e0ce35bddfdb0014e82b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen32270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32271" type="x-p"/> My sheep wandered through all the mountains - They all became idolaters, and lost the knowledge of the true God. And could it be otherwise while they had such pastors? "Himself a wanderer from the narrow way; <div eID="gen32271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32272" type="x-p"/> His silly sheep, no wonder that they stray!" <div eID="gen32272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32273" type="x-p"/> Reader, if thou be a minister, a preacher, or a person in holy orders, or pretended holy orders, or art one pretending to holy orders, look at the qualifications of a good shepherd as laid down by the prophet. <div eID="gen32273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32274" type="x-p"/> 1. He professes to be a shepherd, and to be qualified for the office. <div eID="gen32274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32275" type="x-p"/> 2. In consequence he undertakes the care of a flock. This supposes that he believes the great Bishop of souls has called him to the pastoral office; and that office implies that he is to give all diligence to save the souls of them that hear him. <div eID="gen32275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32276" type="x-p"/> His Qualifications <div eID="gen32276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32277" type="x-p"/> 1. He is skillful; he knows the disease of sin and its consequences; for the Eternal Spirit, by whom he is called, has convinced him of sin, of righteousness, and of judgment. <div eID="gen32277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32278" type="x-p"/> 2. He knows well the great remedy for this disease, the passion and sacrificial death of the Lord Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen32278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32279" type="x-p"/> 3. He is skillful, and knows how to apply this remedy. <div eID="gen32279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32280" type="x-p"/> 4. The flock over which he watches is, in its individuals, either, - <div eID="gen32280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32281" type="x-p"/> 1. Healthy and sound. <div eID="gen32281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32282" type="x-p"/> 2. Or, in a state of convalescence, returning to health. <div eID="gen32282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32283" type="x-p"/> 3. Or, still under the whole power of the general disease. <div eID="gen32283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32284" type="x-p"/> 4. Or, some are dying in a state of spiritual weakness. <div eID="gen32284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32285" type="x-p"/> 5. Or, some are fallen into sin, and sorely bruised and broken in their souls by that fall. <div eID="gen32285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32286" type="x-p"/> 6. Or, some have been driven away by some sore temptation or cruel usage. <div eID="gen32286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32287" type="x-p"/> 7. Or, some have wandered from the flock, are got into strange pastures, and are perverted by erroneous doctrines. Or, <div eID="gen32287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32288" type="x-p"/> 8. Some wolf has got among them, and scattered the whole flock. Now, the true shepherd, the pastor of God's choosing, knows: - <div eID="gen32288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32289" type="x-p"/> 1. How to keep the healthy in health; and cause them to grow in grace, and in the knowledge of Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen32289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32290" type="x-p"/> 2. How to nourish, feed, and care for the convalescent, that they may be brought into a state of spiritual soundness. <div eID="gen32290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32291" type="x-p"/> 3. How to reprove, instruct, and awaken those who are still under the full power of the disease of sin. <div eID="gen32291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32292" type="x-p"/> 4. How to find out and remove the cause of all that spiritual weakness of which he sees some slowly dying. <div eID="gen32292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32293" type="x-p"/> 5. How to deal with those who have fallen into some scandalous sin, and restore them from their fall. <div eID="gen32293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32294" type="x-p"/> 6. How to find out and turn aside the sore temptation or cruel usage by which some have been driven away. <div eID="gen32294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32295" type="x-p"/> 7. How to seek and bring back to the fold those who have strayed into strange pastures, and have had their souls perverted by erroneous doctrines; and knows also how, by a godly discipline, to preserve him in the flock, and keep the flock honourably together. <div eID="gen32295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32296" type="x-p"/> 8. How to oppose, confound, and expel the grievous wolf, who has got among the flock, and is scattering them from each other, and from God. He knows how to preach, explain, and defend the truth. He is well acquainted with the weapons he is to use, and the spirit in which he is to employ them. <div eID="gen32296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32297" type="x-p"/> In a word, the true shepherd gives up his life to the sheep; spends and is spent for the glory of God; and gives up his life for the sheep, in defense of them, and in laboring for their welfare. And while he is thus employed, it is the duty of the flock to feed and clothe him; and see that neither he nor his family lack the necessaries and conveniencies of life. The laborer is worthy of his meat. He who does not labor, or, because of his ignorance of God and salvation, cannot labor, in the word and doctrine, deserves neither meat nor drink; and if he exact that by law, which he has not honestly earned by a proper discharge of the pastoral function, let him read this chapter, and learn from it what a fearful account he shall have to give to the chief Shepherd at the great day; and what a dreadful punishment shall be inflicted on him, when the blood of the souls lost through his neglect or inefficiency is visited upon him! See the notes on <reference osisRef="Eze.3.17">Eze 3:17</reference>, etc.
entries.334543986410a8c15bfae50977a79135bc6e0ef0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen32297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32298" type="x-p"/> Therefore, ye shepherds, (ye bad and wicked shepherds), hear the word of the Lord - In the preceding character of the good shepherd the reader will find, by reversing the particulars, the character of a bad shepherd; and therefore I may be excused from entering into farther detail.
entries.7d80563708691ea233caf57013788afc35d297b9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen32298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32299" type="x-p"/> I will - cause them to cease from feeding the flock - God, in this country, unpriested a whole hierarchy who fed not the flock, but ruled them with force and cruelty; and he raised up a new set of shepherds better qualified, both by sound doctrine and learning, to feed the flock. Let these be faithful, lest God cause them to cease, and raise up other feeders.
entries.8ab0fe327eeae991afc1bfd6b9e2f50eb4f2e9bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen32299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32300" type="x-p"/> Cloudy and dark day - Times of general distress and persecution; in such times the shepherd should be especially watchful.
entries.be75a74849a8d28160ed77ffbedf8a1c966d0cb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32301" type="x-p"/> I will - feed them upon the mountains - When I bring back the people from their captivity, I will raise up to them a holy and diligent priesthood, who shall in all places give them sound instruction. But this, and some of the following promises, belong to the Christian Church, as we shall find below.
entries.0b1337e726629ea2b37556b53f3ccfe57917b870: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen32301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32302" type="x-p"/> I will destroy the fat and the strong - I will destroy those cruel and imperious shepherds who abuse their authority, and tyrannize over the flock.
entries.f82fa17148ae6d1584aebfbcbccb3328b3f5d747: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32303" type="x-p"/> And as for you, O my flock - After having spoken to the shepherds, he now addresses the flock. <div eID="gen32303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32304" type="x-p"/> I judge between cattle and cattle - Between false and true professors; between them that have only the form and them that have the power of godliness; between the backslider in heart and the upright man.
